text: Lesson 5 covered the simple case: the attacker types directly into the chat box. This lesson covers the one that should actually worry you more — indirect prompt injection, where the end user never types anything suspicious at all. They ask a completely normal question, and the system goes and fetches content that was already sitting there, built to be read as a command.

It's the same underlying weakness as direct injection — an LLM that can't structurally tell instructions apart from data — just exploited through a different route. The malicious text is planted somewhere the model will retrieve and process on someone else's behalf: a web page, a PDF, an email, a product review. OWASP's LLM01 category covers this explicitly as a subtype of prompt injection, right alongside the direct case.

Think through the real ingestion paths. A RAG pipeline pulls document chunks into context before answering. A browsing agent summarizes a fetched web page. An email-triage assistant reads an inbox and drafts replies. A coding assistant reads repository comments and README files. In every one of those, content no human personally vetted carries the exact same authority, as far as the model's concerned, as the developer's own instructions.

That's what makes it harder to catch. A content filter built to watch user chat messages never sees the paragraph sitting inside a document the RAG pipeline just indexed. And because the injected text can sit dormant in a shared store, it can compromise a completely different user's unrelated query days or weeks later — a stored, multi-hop exposure direct injection doesn't have.

So when you're investigating unexpected behavior, don't stop at what the user typed. Ask what the model retrieved right before it acted — an action with no clear link back to the actual request, right after a browsing or document-lookup step, is worth tracing back to its source. Lesson 7 picks up from here, and tackles the obvious-looking fix that doesn't actually work: filtering that content for bad words.
